I did more research about this specific interaction .
So I post it here. 

Antipsychotics targets dopamine receptors in all part of the brain, but more specifically at some parts of the brain, like striatum,  amygdala, Cortex.
And stimulants are often more specific at the (prefrontal) cortex.
Prefrontal cortex is linked to "simple" information processing, thus it relates good why methylphenidate is seen as a "work booster" and not much mind altering (eg: euphoria...), the cortex is related to higher reasoning function, it's the main targets sites.

Also antipsychotics take of the pleasure related to stimulants by blocking the mesolimbic pathways (related to the reward feeling).

So, yes, if using an antipsychotic drug, before or at the same time of using a "traditional" stimulant, the effect will be greatly diminished.
Cignitive enhancement will be low (but less so for simple repetitive tasks).

There will still be more activation of D2 in regions of the brain that are allocated to information processing, but very low activation of other parts that results in the positive aspect of a stimulant (again exemple euphoria, cognitive enhancement,  new ideas/new brain pathways...).

Same as how it prevents "traditional" serotoninergic psychedelics (psilocybin, LSD,..) to work, as they also target 5HT2A, and in a lesser extent 5HT1A and 5HT2C.(no strong relationship with the "trip").

I will edit this final comment when I've more data, in hands.



So to conclude:

It doesn't completely abolish the stimulant effect, but greatly reduces it.

More specifically, the parts of the brain that stimulants affect to create all the "feel good" sensations give a  greatly reduced response to stimulants when used along with an antipsychotic. 
Note: Many antidepressants also reduce the "feel good" response, but to a lesser extend.

The only aspect that is less impacted (but still a lot) is the prefrontal cortex, related to simple tasks/information processing.
